title: Visiting Goindval
hookLine: the step-well of Guru Amar Das

cards: The light changes halfway down. At the top of the stairs it's a bright Punjab afternoon, dust and noise and a river nearby. A few steps lower, the walls close in, the air turns cool, and the street drops away.
Lower still, there's water, dark and still, at the bottom of a deep shaft of stone. People go down barefoot, one step at a time, some of them saying something under their breath on every step.
This is the baoli, the step-well, at Goindval Sahib.

teach.b: Begin with the place. Goindval is a town on the Beas river, the home of Guru Amar Das, the third Guru.
Tradition says he had the baoli dug there, so people could reach water in a dry land, and it became a gathering place for Sikhs. Then the purpose.
A step-well is a practical thing: water sits deep below the ground, so you build stairs down to it. But a Guru's well was never only plumbing.
Tradition says the water was open to everyone, whatever their caste, and that openness was itself a teaching. Next, the custom.
Some pilgrims recite the Japji Sahib once on every step as they go down, slowly, all the way to the water. It is slow on purpose. Finally, the Guru's word underneath.
In the Japji, Guru Nanak says, in paraphrase, that along this path are the steps of a stairway, and by climbing them one becomes one with the Lord.
The Japji's stairs go up; the well's stairs go down.
Both say the same thing about how it's done: not in a leap, but one step, then the next, then the next. The baoli at Goindval Sahib still has its stairs, its water, and its slow walkers.

how: Pilgrims visit the baoli at Goindval Sahib, and some recite the Japji Sahib once on each step as they go down to the water, then bathe.

games.q: you're at the top of the baoli's stairs, and you've heard about the custom. what do some pilgrims do?
o: hurry down to reach the water first.
recite the Japji once on every step, all the way down.

games.why: some pilgrims recite the Japji once on each step. it is slow on purpose.

practice: Go to some stairs if they're near, or take a few slow steps across the room, letting each foot land fully before the next and breathing out on every step.
If you know a line of the Japji, say it under your breath as you go; if not, just count your breaths, slower than feels normal.

wordCard.voice: Visiting Goindval. The town of Guru Amar Das on the Beas, and its baoli, where some pilgrims recite the Japji on every step down to the water. Today's word.
